Directions: Today you will read two articles about rocks. Read the article, then answer each question that follows.
Title: Collecting Rocks
Author: by Rachel M. Barker
Content: Geologists classify rocks in `text(three)` groups, according to the major `text(Earth)` processes that formed them. The `text(three)` rock groups are igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks. Anyone who wishes to collect rocks should become familiar with the characteristics of these `text(three)` rock groups. Knowing how a geologist classifies rocks is important if you want to transform a random group of rock specimens into a true collection.

Igneous rocks are formed from melted rock that has cooled and solidified. When rocks are buried deep within the `text(Earth)`, they melt because of the high pressure and temperature; the molten rock (called magma) can then flow upward or even be erupted from a volcano onto the `text(Earth's)` surface. When magma cools slowly, usually at depths of `text(thousands)` of `text(feet)`, crystals grow from the molten liquid, and a coarse-grained rock forms. When magma cools rapidly, usually at or near the `text(Earth's)` surface, the crystals are extremely small, and a fine-grained rock results. A wide variety of rocks are formed by different cooling rates and different chemical compositions of the original magma. Obsidian (volcanic glass), granite, basalt, and andesite porphyry are `text(four)` of the many types of igneous rock.

Sedimentary rocks are formed at the surface of the `text(Earth)`, either in water or on land. They are layered accumulations of sediments-fragments of rocks, minerals, or animal or plant material. Temperatures and pressures are low at the `text(Earth's)` surface, and sedimentary rocks show this fact by their appearance and the minerals they contain. Most sedimentary rocks become cemented together by minerals and chemicals or are held together by electrical attraction; some, however, remain loose and unconsolidated. The layers are normally parallel or nearly parallel to the `text(Earth's)` surface; if they are at high angles to the surface or are twisted or broken, some kind of `text(Earth)` movement has occurred since the rock was formed. Sedimentary rocks are forming around us all the time. Sand and gravel on beaches or in river bars look like the sandstone and conglomerate they will become. Compacted and dried mud flats harden into shale. Scuba divers who have seen mud and shells settling on the floors of lagoons find it easy to understand how sedimentary rocks form.

Sometimes sedimentary and igneous rocks are subjected to pressures so intense or heat so high that they are completely changed. They become metamorphic rocks, which form while deeply buried within the `text(Earth's)` crust. The process of metamorphism does not melt the rocks, but instead transforms them into denser, more compact rocks. New minerals are created either by rearrangement of mineral components or by reactions with fluids that enter the rocks. Some kinds of metamorphic rocks-granite gneiss and biotite schist are `text(two)` examples - are strongly banded or foliated. (Foliated means the parallel arrangement of certain mineral grains that gives the rock a striped appearance.) Pressure or temperature can even change previously metamorphosed rocks into new types.
